messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Six years ago, the controlled industrial burn at the regional printing facility Kane had been auditing for a major distribution contract catastrophically failed. The sudden collapse of the ventilation stacks and the roar of chemical-fed flames had sealed the loading bays. He had watched through heat-warped glass as the structure groaned, the weight of the disaster settling into his bones. In the years since, Kane’s internal landscape has been dominated by unbidden, high-definition photographs of the event. These graphic visual memories, which force their way into his mind when he least expects them, have directly dictated his survival strategies. Because the images remain so vivid and inescapable, he has felt compelled to avoid seeing his old publishing colleagues, fearing that unprocessed trauma will overwhelm him, while also finding himself constantly scanning the environment for structural instability. The uncontrolled access of these memories means that ordinary cues now act as potent catalysts; a casual discussion about the plant’s collapse or the faint, sweet odor of alcohol on a stranger’s hands instantly hijacks his attention, pulling him back to the loading bay with visceral dread. His nervous system never received the memo that the danger had passed. The persistent jumpy state and violent startle response he experiences to ordinary noises have kept his threat perception chronically elevated. This unrelenting alertness, which now clings to him even inside his own home, has further fortified his need for environmental control. Sitting with his back pressed against a wall allows him to monitor the room, a physical manifestation of his internal hyperarousal that leaves him perpetually braced. His persistent startle response and general jumpy state keep his threat system hyperactive, which directly lowers his threshold for traumatic recall, allowing the graphic visual memories to surface with greater frequency. The exhausting routine of checking surroundings and maintaining rigid seating arrangements prevents his brain from updating the trauma, leaving the memories uncontrolled and perpetually raw. The physiological toll of these safety behaviors drains his autonomic nervous system, ensuring he remains jumpy and easily startled by everyday sounds like a closing cabinet or a passing truck. By isolating himself from his former network, Kane has deprived himself of professional and social perspective, which means that when triggers do occur, they bypass his usual defenses and strike with disproportionate intensity. He had come to believe that if he ever stopped scanning the exits or relaxing his shoulders against the wall, the disaster would simply resume. At sixty-three, Kane’s days as a senior publisher are now governed by these invisible boundaries. He reviews manuscript layouts from his home office, yet his attention is perpetually divided between the digital proofs on his screen and the street below his window. The cycle of checking, avoiding, and hyperarousal has eroded his professional confidence and strained his marriage. It was his wife’s quiet observation that he was disappearing behind his own defenses that finally brought him to my office. He sat on the edge of the chair, his hands flat on his knees, admitting that he desperately wanted to read a book again without searching the perimeter for threats, though he remained terrified that without his vigilance, he would never wake up again.
